title: British Ceylon
capsule: The medieval Sinhalese kingdoms of Ceylon fragmented after the fall of Polonnaruwa (c. 1235) into competing courts at Dambadeniya, Yapahu, Kurunegala, and ultimately Kotte, as South Indian Tamil dynasties pressed from the north and local strongmen contested the interior. The Kotte kingdom reached its greatest extent under Parakramabahu VI (r. 1412–1467), who reunified the island for the last time and sponsored a literary renaissance in Sinhala. After his death the realm broke into rival courts at Kotte, Sitawaka, and Kandy; Portuguese caravels first called at Colombo in 1505–1506, and by 1507 the Estado da India had secured cinnamon tribute from Kotte, marking the end of medieval Ceylonese autonomy.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Medieval Ceylonese territorial extent is moderately attested through Sinhala chronicles (Cūḷavaṃsa), epigraphy, and early Portuguese reports, but internal boundaries between competing kingdoms are reconstructed with significant uncertainty.
